title: India set for 'unparalleled' decades-long growth, says Tata chief Chandrasekaran
excerpt: Speaking at Sai University's convocation in Chennai, the Tata Sons chairman said AI would create industries that don't exist today and told graduates to treat careers as marathons — while arguing India's economic rise could run for decades.
body:
• N Chandrasekaran, chairman of Tata Sons, told graduates at Chennai's Sai University convocation on Saturday that India is entering a period of economic growth "unparalleled in our own history and unparalleled with any part of the world."
  • He said artificial intelligence, technology and regulatory change are reshaping the global economy — and that AI will open new industries "which don't exist today" even as it displaces existing jobs.
  • Chandrasekaran urged graduates to "run dual races" — pursuing long-term goals alongside shorter-term achievements — and framed careers as marathons measured by continuous improvement, not comparisons.
  • The remarks carry weight beyond campus: he has led the Tata Group since 2017, overseeing investment of ₹5.5 lakh crore and a tripling of market capitalization.

India is on the cusp of economic expansion that could run "unparalleled" for decades, Tata Sons Chairman N Chandrasekaran said Saturday, urging a new generation of graduates to prepare for an era in which artificial intelligence creates entire industries that do not yet exist. Addressing the Sai University convocation in Chennai as chief guest, he said India stood in "a very strong position" as AI, technology and regulatory changes reshape the global economy.

"You are stepping into a world which has a very changing global economic, technological, disruptive, AI led revolutionary, regulatory and other changes that are constantly evolving," Chandrasekaran said, according to ANI. He acknowledged the growing anxiety around AI-driven job losses, but argued the technology would simultaneously unlock opportunities that are difficult to anticipate. "The world is full to the brim with possibilities," he said, adding that "five years from now there will be industries which don't exist today."

"Unparalleled in our own history and unparalleled with any part of the world."

— N Chandrasekaran, Tata Sons Chairman, at the Sai University convocation

Context & Background

Chandrasekaran took charge of Tata Sons in January 2017 after a three-decade career at TCS, succeeding Ratan Tata in the wake of the Cyrus Mistry ouster. His tenure has been defined by large, capital-intensive bets: the re-entry into aviation through the Air India acquisition, a push into semiconductors and electronics manufacturing through Tata Electronics, battery gigafactories in India and the UK, and digital businesses under Tata Digital.

The numbers behind the optimism are substantial. Under his leadership, the group invested ₹5.5 lakh crore, nearly doubled revenue and tripled both net profits and market capitalization. For FY25, revenue across all listed and unlisted entities reached ₹15.34 lakh crore, with net profit at ₹1.13 lakh crore. Chandrasekaran's own tenure as chairman is set to conclude in February 2027.

Impact & Analysis

Chandrasekaran's forecast adds a prominent corporate voice to India's growth narrative at a moment when global capital is actively reweighting toward the country. His framing — growth and AI disruption arriving together — reflects how India's largest conglomerates are positioning themselves: betting that a domestic consumption engine plus a technology buildout can compound for decades, rather than riding a single export cycle.

The optimism is not unqualified. His own legacy includes bets still in the investment or turnaround phase, and the group's market capitalization has shed value over the past year as TCS shares declined. The AI transition he describes as opportunity is the same force pressuring the IT services revenues that underwrote much of the group's recent performance — a tension his "dual races" advice, aimed at graduates, applies to the conglomerate itself.

"You have got to measure yourself on progress, continuous improvement, push yourself towards what you want to do."

— N Chandrasekaran, Tata Sons Chairman

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora, Chandrasekaran's outlook is more than rhetoric — it shapes where overseas Indians direct capital, careers and startup ambitions. A decades-long India growth story is the backdrop against which NRIs weigh investing back home versus abroad, and his AI-first framing signals which sectors will reward that bet.

What's Next

The test of Chandrasekaran's "unparalleled" thesis will be execution: whether Tata's semiconductor, electronics and AI bets mature into profitable businesses, and whether India's economy absorbs AI-driven job churn without losing its demographic dividend. With his chairmanship ending in February 2027, his successor inherits both the forecast and the responsibility of delivering it. The graduates at Sai University, meanwhile, get a head start on the industries that don't exist yet.
